section_summary: This section combines translated Japanese and colonial immigration regulations with consular correspondence about their administration. It includes extensive Taiwan rules governing Chinese laborers and alien entry, followed by a detailed 1933 dispute over Yokohama police delaying the S.S. President Jefferson after an immigration-inspection misunderstanding. The final pages begin a 1934 report surveying Japanese emigration, immigration, overseas settlement, and foreign restrictions on Japanese migrants.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 179 Transmitting Japanese Alien-Entry Regulations
subfiles.about: Transmits translations of the alien-entry laws applying to Japan and the Japanese South Seas Mandate.
subfiles.summary: Forbes responds to the Department's circular instruction of January 30, 1931, by forwarding two translated sets of alien-entry regulations. He notes that the corresponding law for the Kwantung Leased Territory and South Manchuria Railway Zone had already been sent by the American consul at Dairen in 1918.

subfiles.title: Regulations Governing the Entry of Aliens into Japan
subfiles.about: Sets the passport, visa, exclusion, inspection, and deportation rules for aliens entering Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ordinance lets governors exclude aliens lacking passports, suspected enemies, threats to order or morals, paupers, those with dangerous diseases or likely public charges; it requires photographs and Japanese consular visas, truthful answers and deportation for fraud; diplomats and ship crews exempt; amended 1921 and 1924.

subfiles.title: Matters Relating to the Entry of Aliens into the South Sea Islands
subfiles.about: Extends passport-based alien admission and exclusion controls to the Japanese South Seas Mandate.
subfiles.summary: South Sea Islands ordinance, gazetted May 13, 1925, mirrors the home-islands rules: branch chiefs may exclude aliens without valid documents or dangerous, indigent or diseased ones, requiring passports with Japanese visas, with deportation for fraud and exemptions for diplomats and crews.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Tokyo Despatch No. 114
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file containing a report on Japanese immigration laws.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Hutchinson's Tokyo Despatch 114 (November 18, 1932) transmitting a report on Japan's immigration laws, file 800.504/36.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Translations of Taiwan Immigration Laws
subfiles.from: Charles L. De Vault, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Transmits comprehensive translations of Taiwan's laws governing Chinese laborers, other Chinese entrants, and aliens generally.
subfiles.summary: De Vault says the 1910 Chinese laborer regulations remain largely in force while other immigrant restrictions ended in 1921; local officers keep wide discretion, there's no significant Chinese immigration problem, and 1924 admissions were 6,819 laborers and 3,543 non-laborers.

subfiles.title: Regulations Governing Chinese Laborers
subfiles.about: Regulates the recruitment, documentation, landing, employment, support, and deportation of Chinese laborers in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Chinese manual laborers needed sailing certificates from licensed agents and landing permits in Taiwan; agents posted security, screened applicants, gave relief and paid deportation costs; harmful persons could be deported and violators fined; amendments through 1920 changed provisions such as security.

subfiles.title: Regulations Regarding Enforcement of the Regulations Governing Chinese Laborers
subfiles.to: Provincial and prefectural governments in Taiwan
subfiles.about: Provides administrative procedures for examining, documenting, supervising, and deporting Chinese laborers.
subfiles.summary: Enforcement instruction: officials examine arriving laborers and certificates, record admissions and issue landing permits, investigate agent license applicants, and may deport categories like quack vendors, fortune tellers and habitual thieves, keeping deportees under police surveillance and notifying Japanese consuls in China.

subfiles.title: Form No. 1: Register of Landing Permits Granted to Chinese Laborers
subfiles.about: Provides a register for recording landing permits issued to Chinese laborers.
subfiles.summary: Blank Form 1, register of landing permits for Chinese laborers: permit number, native place, name, age, labor type, landing port and agent.

subfiles.title: Form No. 2: Landing Permit
subfiles.about: Provides the official landing permit issued to an admitted Chinese laborer.
subfiles.summary: Blank Form 2, landing permit for Chinese laborers, with name, age, occupation, port, agent, photograph space, seal and Chinese-language provisions.

subfiles.title: Form No. 3: Report on Chinese Laborers Deported
subfiles.about: Provides a standardized report for individual deportations of Chinese laborers.
subfiles.summary: Blank Form 3, report on Chinese laborers deported, for provincial or prefectural reports to the Taiwan Government-General.

subfiles.title: Form No. 4: Monthly List of Chinese Laborers Landed in or Returned from Taiwan
subfiles.about: Provides a monthly statistical table for Chinese laborers entering or leaving Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Blank Form 4, monthly list of Chinese laborers landed in or returned from Taiwan, by native place, sex and occupation, with columns for Canton, Fuzhou and Xiamen.

subfiles.title: Regulations Governing Entry of Aliens in Taiwan
subfiles.about: Establishes general passport, exclusion, inspection, and deportation rules for aliens arriving in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Taiwan entry regulations let governors refuse undocumented aliens, suspected enemies, threats to order, paupers, those with dangerous diseases or likely public charges; passports normally need photographs and a recent Japanese visa; police may demand documents and deport fraud users; diplomats and ship crews exempt.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the President Jefferson Incident
subfiles.about: Reviews the Yokohama detention of the S.S. President Jefferson and recommends no further action.
subfiles.summary: Memo on the President Jefferson incident: a junior deck officer first kept plainclothes police and immigration officers from boarding during quarantine, and Yokohama authorities restricted communication until Consul De Vault intervened; after a satisfactory local settlement the file is kept only for reference.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 132: Detention of the S.S. President Jefferson in Yokohama Harbor
subfiles.from: Charles L. De Vault, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports the three-hour restriction of an American passenger vessel by Yokohama Harbor Police and the negotiated settlement.
subfiles.summary: De Vault explains that junior deck officer Robert Sweetser mistakenly barred plainclothes immigration officers from boarding while the vessel was under quarantine inspection. The police retaliated by restricting passengers, cargo handling, fueling, and other activities until the consul secured the vessel's release. De Vault considered the police response excessive but acknowledged the ship officer's poor judgment and found no political, racial, or anti-American motive. He handled the dispute locally and obtained assurances satisfactory to the ship, its management, the embassy, and the Tokyo consulate general.

subfiles.title: De Vault's Initial Letter Concerning the Boarding Misunderstanding
subfiles.about: Expresses regret for the misunderstanding that prevented Japanese immigration officers from boarding the President Jefferson.
subfiles.summary: De Vault explains the quartermaster didn't understand Japanese and couldn't identify the plainclothes officers without badges; they were invited aboard once identified but declined, and he hopes it won't recur.

subfiles.title: Captain Lustie's Letter Concerning the Boarding Misunderstanding
subfiles.about: Explains the captain's view of the mistaken refusal to admit Japanese immigration officers.
subfiles.summary: Captain Lustie repeats that language difficulties and the officers' lack of uniforms or badges caused the misunderstanding, and says ship's officers meant no interference and believed they were obeying quarantine rules.

subfiles.title: Robert Sweetser's Letter Concerning the Boarding Misunderstanding
subfiles.about: Gives the junior deck officer's written explanation of why he initially refused entry to plainclothes immigration officers.
subfiles.summary: Robert Sweetser says the officers wore no uniforms or badges and weren't identifiable, he meant no obstruction, and ship's personnel were trying to comply with quarantine rules.

subfiles.title: American Mail Line Protest over Delay to the President Jefferson
subfiles.about: Protests the harbor police restrictions that delayed the President Jefferson's passengers, cargo work, and refueling.
subfiles.summary: American Mail Line's Thompson protests that after unidentified officials were admitted, they refused to begin passport examination or allow stevedores and fuel suppliers aboard until 11:45 a.m., endangering the Kobe and Shanghai schedule with substantial loss; he asks confirmation the police action was unwarranted and assurances.

subfiles.title: Formal Consular Protest over the President Jefferson's Detention
subfiles.about: Presents a detailed protest against the police restriction of the vessel, its officers, passengers, cargo operations, and shore access.
subfiles.summary: De Vault characterizes the restriction as an unjustified virtual arrest that interfered with fueling, cargo handling, immigration processing, and the work of the captain, general agent, and port captain. He reconstructs the boarding misunderstanding, emphasizing the plainclothes officers' failure to identify themselves and Sweetser's immediate effort to reverse his refusal. The protest also describes repeated police demands for written admissions or apologies before the vessel was released following consular telephone intervention. Although De Vault rejects suggestions of anti-foreign, racial, or political motives, he requests firm measures preventing any recurrence.

subfiles.title: Governor Yokoyama's Reply to the American Mail Line
subfiles.about: Defends the immigration officers and disputes the company's account of the President Jefferson incident.
subfiles.summary: Governor Yokoyama says immigration officers boarded early for convenience but were forcibly prevented from working, though plain clothes, police books, an official launch and company identification should have established them; he denies the passport dispute caused the stevedore inspection, won't guarantee non-recurrence, and suggests examining ships at the pier.

subfiles.title: De Vault's Proposed Understanding on the President Jefferson Incident
subfiles.about: Seeks written confirmation of a conciliatory interpretation and settlement of the harbor incident.
subfiles.summary: De Vault says the affair was a mutual misunderstanding mostly from language, records an understanding that both ship personnel and Japanese authorities will be told to observe courtesies, and seeks confirmation Japan didn't mean to restrict or discriminate against American shipping.

subfiles.title: Governor Yokoyama's Confirmation of Settlement
subfiles.about: Confirms the agreed characterization of the incident as a mutual misunderstanding and promises preventive instructions.
subfiles.summary: Yokoyama concurs with De Vault's February 24 letter, regrets the incident as mutual misunderstanding, promises careful instructions to officials, and asks the consul to inform the ship's officers.

subfiles.title: Port Report—Yokohama, Voyage No. 40 West
subfiles.about: Reports the boarding dispute, police-imposed delay, cargo operations, fueling, and passenger movements during the President Jefferson's Yokohama call.
subfiles.summary: Lustie's port report: plainclothes officers failed to board during quarantine, Sweetser tried to correct it, police held back stevedores and passengers until De Vault intervened and release came at 11:45 a.m., leaving Kobe departure two days and three hours late; the consul will seek assurances against interference.

subfiles.title: Robert Sweetser's Report on the Immigration-Officer Incident
subfiles.about: Provides Sweetser's first-person account of his encounter with the plainclothes immigration officers.
subfiles.summary: Sweetser, posted at the accommodation ladder to exclude unauthorized persons, admitted uniformed officials but questioned unidentified men in civilian clothes with no identification; after Neitman said they were immigration officers, they tried to explain but the launch had left.

subfiles.title: Department of State Acknowledgment of the President Jefferson Settlement
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Approves the mutually satisfactory and unpublicized resolution of the Yokohama incident.
subfiles.summary: State, citing De Vault's Despatch 132 of February 28, 1933, is gratified the President Jefferson incident was adjusted to mutual satisfaction without publicity.

subfiles.title: Trend of Migratory Movements—Japan
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul; approved by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.about: Begins a broad study of Japanese emigration, immigration, colonial settlement, and foreign immigration restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The title page and contents outline a report covering Japanese migration to Brazil, other parts of South America, Asia, Manchukuo, and the Philippines, as well as immigration into Japan and restrictive legislation. The introduction traces migration from Hawaii and the United States to the growing government-directed movement toward Brazil, while comparing overseas Japanese populations with foreign and Korean migration into Japan. It discusses exclusionary measures in the United States, Canada, and Australia and identifies Japanese emigration as a controlled instrument of government policy. The historical section begins with Tokugawa isolation, Commodore Perry's arrival, early Hawaiian migration, the Gentlemen's Agreement, and the subsequent restriction of passport issuance; the report continues beyond page 72.
